newsitem.title: UK: Scientists find way of targeting tumours.
newsitem.headline: Scientists find way of targeting tumours.

text.p: Scientists have found a new way of targeting malignant growths by using genetically modified cells to deliver tumour-killing toxins.

In a letter to the latest edition of Nature magazine, published on Thursday, the U.S.-based scientists said the new approach could be useful to treat cancerous tumours, autoimmune diseases and hazardous viral infections.

The scientists used lymphocytes, a kind of white blood cell, which they genetically modified to turn them into tumour-specific "killer cells", Si-Yi Chen, from the Bowman Gray Medical School in North Carolina, and her colleagues wrote.
The scientists homed in on a protein known as HER-2 produced on the surface of breast, ovarian and other tumours.

The lymphocytes were modified to make a toxin linked to an antibody specific to the HER-2 protein. The lymphocytes infiltrated the tumour, the toxins were then guided by the antibody to the cells expressing HER-2 and killed the tumour.

The new approach was designed to combat the problems of the limited access of antibodies to solid tumours and the difficulty in obtaining tumour-specific killer lymphocytes, which have prevented all but limited success in tumour immunotherapy.
"Our approach, which has features of both antibody-directed and cell-mediated immunotherapy, may have application in a gene therapy context," the scientists wrote.
